sources.news_title: Eaton Fire Exhibited Millions to Extremely High Lead Levels
sources.text:
Eaton Fire Exposed Millions to Extremely High Lead Levels
|                                                       By                             Bob Cronin                                 withNewser.AI                                                                                   Posted Oct 28, 2026  7:05 PM CDT                                                       | 
Millions of Los Angeles-area residents apparently inhaled far more than ash during last year's Eaton Fire. A new Caltech study published in the journal Science Advances found that at the blaze's height, roughly 7 million people were breathing lead levels about 80 times what's normally in the air—where concentrations are usually near zero. Lead, a neurotoxin, was just one ingredient in what researchers call a cocktail of contaminants that included arsenic, chlorine, bromine, zinc, and copper, the Washington Post reports.
The fire burned through a heavily developed area, and its smoke carried some 50 times more lead than that from the more rural 2024 Airport Fire, the study says. Scientists warn they still don't know the long-term health fallout, and note that exposure didn't end when the flames were extinguished, with toxic metals later detected in air, soil, and even indoors. "We're seeing that climate change is absolutely increasing these events," said lead author Haroula Baliaka. An expert who wasn't involved in the study, per the AP, said it's a reminder of a "strange and increasingly dangerous new world" where urban and wildland intersect—and increasingly catch fire.

sources.news_title: Los Angeles Wildfire Smoke Exposed Nearly 7 Million People to Lead Levels 80 Times Above Normal, Study Finds
sources.text:
A new California Institute of Technology study reveals that smoke from the devastating 2025 Eaton Fire contained sharply elevated concentrations of lead, arsenic and other toxic substances, exposing millions of Los Angeles residents to pollution levels far above normal.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
LOS ANGELES — Nearly 7 million people across the Los Angeles metropolitan area were exposed to airborne lead concentrations approximately 80 times higher than normal during a 24-hour period at the height of the January 2025 Eaton Fire, according to a new study examining the toxic chemicals released when wildfires destroy homes and other structures.
The research, published Wednesday, Oct. 28, in the journal Science Advances, found that smoke from the Eaton Fire contained substantially higher concentrations of hazardous metals and chemical compounds than smoke produced by fires burning primarily through vegetation.
Scientists at the California Institute of Technology determined that the urban fire plume contained more than 50 times as much lead, seven times as much chlorine and bromine, and three times as much arsenic as smoke from a predominantly wildland fire.
The findings, detailed in a Caltech announcement, highlight the additional health hazards created when wildfires spread into residential communities, burning vehicles, buildings, household chemicals and electronic equipment.
“The main, key finding is really that wildfire smoke is very different fundamentally from the urban smoke,” said Nga Lee “Sally” Ng, a study co-author and Caltech environmental science and engineering professor.
Ng said advanced monitoring technology allowed scientists to “actually see the very detailed component of these particles that we are breathing.”
The Eaton Fire began Jan. 7, 2025, in the foothills above Altadena, northeast of Los Angeles. Strong winds rapidly pushed the flames into residential neighborhoods, destroying thousands of homes and businesses.
The Eaton and Palisades fires together killed at least 31 people and destroyed more than 16,000 structures, making them among the most destructive disasters in California history.
Researchers said the destruction of manufactured materials created a chemically different type of smoke than that produced when forests, grasslands and other vegetation burn.
To investigate those differences, scientists analyzed measurements collected at an air-monitoring station in Pico Rivera, approximately 11 miles south of Altadena.
The station belongs to the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork, known as ASCENT, a National Science Foundation-funded network of 12 monitoring locations.
Unlike conventional air-quality monitoring systems that may collect samples only periodically, ASCENT equipment can measure the chemical composition of fine airborne particles, known as PM2.5, at hourly intervals.
That capability allowed researchers to track changes in smoke composition as the Eaton Fire moved through developed neighborhoods and into surrounding mountain areas.
The highest concentrations of lead occurred Jan. 8 and 9, when large numbers of homes and vehicles were burning.
Using those measurements and population data, researchers estimated that approximately 7 million residents experienced 24-hour average lead concentrations more than 80 times typical background levels.
The estimate describes elevated airborne lead exposure, not confirmed lead poisoning among those residents.
Scientists compared the Eaton Fire measurements with data from the 2024 Airport Fire in Riverside County, which burned predominantly through undeveloped vegetation.
The comparison revealed that urban smoke contained dramatically higher concentrations of several potentially harmful substances.
Lead can originate from older building materials, paint and other manufactured products. Arsenic and other metals may be released when treated materials, vehicles and household contents burn.
The researchers also identified substantial increases in chlorine and bromine, chemical elements associated with certain plastics, flame retardants and other manufactured materials.
Study lead author Haroula Baliaka said the findings demonstrate why urban fires require different approaches to understanding smoke pollution.
“Urban fire plumes are chemically distinct from those of wildfires. Now that we have these observational data about how they differ, we can go back and adjust our models to more accurately estimate how smoke might affect people,” Baliaka said.
Researchers also observed that the chemical composition of the smoke changed as the fire progressed.
During the initial destruction of Altadena neighborhoods, lead concentrations increased sharply relative to potassium, an element commonly released when vegetation burns.
As the flames moved toward forested mountain areas, lead concentrations declined relative to potassium, indicating a transition toward a more typical wildfire smoke signature.
The changing chemical measurements helped researchers distinguish pollution associated with burning structures from emissions produced by burning vegetation.
The health implications remain an important unanswered question.
Lead is a neurotoxin associated with impaired neurological development in children, reduced cognitive performance and increased blood pressure in adults. Arsenic exposure has been linked to several cancers.
However, much of the existing research examines prolonged or repeated exposure rather than brief periods involving unusually high concentrations of multiple toxic substances.
Scientists have not established the precise long-term health consequences of the 24-hour exposure levels documented during the Eaton Fire.
Ed Avol, professor emeritus at the University of Southern California’s Keck School of Medicine, said the findings were consistent with concerns about heavy metals released during urban fires.
The results were “certainly surprising because we haven’t been able to document this sort of thing,” said Avol, who was not involved in the study.
He emphasized the value of having detailed measurements available throughout the fire.
“One of the real advantages of this study is that it had the opportunity to make measurements sort of hour-by-hour across the sampling network,” Avol said.
The research also reinforces concerns raised by previous studies examining the health effects of smoke, ash and debris after destructive urban fires, including the 2023 Maui wildfires.
Yaguang Wei, an environmental medicine researcher at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, said the findings were consistent with evidence suggesting that smoke from fires involving manufactured materials can contain particularly harmful pollutants.
“I think their findings are not surprising,” Wei said.
He argued that governments should invest in improved air monitoring, public warning systems and strategies to reduce wildfire risks.
Researchers noted that expanding development near fire-prone vegetation, combined with hotter and drier conditions associated with climate change, increases the potential for destructive fires where urban and natural environments meet.
The findings suggest that emergency response systems may need to account for the chemical composition of smoke, rather than relying exclusively on measurements of overall particulate pollution.
Baliaka said the research could help improve models used to estimate hazardous exposure and guide public health decisions during future fires.
The study provides evidence that people living far beyond the immediate fire perimeter may encounter hazardous airborne substances when residential neighborhoods burn.
Although the long-term consequences of the Eaton Fire exposures remain uncertain, the researchers said the findings demonstrate the importance of expanding real-time chemical monitoring and adapting emergency planning to the distinctive dangers of urban wildfire smoke.

sources.news_title: Caltech Study Finds Toxic Metals from Eaton Fire
sources.text:
Smoke from the Eaton Fire had a sharply different chemical makeup from typical wildfire smoke, with toxic-metal levels spiking while homes and vehicles burned, according to a Caltech study published Wednesday.
Researchers estimated that nearly 7 million people in the Los Angeles metropolitan area were exposed to 24-hour lead concentrations 80 times higher than typical values at the peak of the fire’s structural burning. The estimate was based on data from an air-monitoring station in Pico Rivera, about 11 miles south of Altadena, that tracked the fire plume.
The study, published in the journal Science Advances, found that the urban plume contained more than 50 times as much lead, seven times as much chlorine and bromine, and three times as much arsenic as typical wildfire smoke.
“Smoke travels; it’s not just about the burn area,” lead author Haroula Baliaka said. “What does a plume mean for people who are miles away from a fire but receive the smoke? We evacuate for fire, but we don’t evacuate for smoke exposure.”
Baliaka and co-author Ryan Ward monitored the plume at the Pico Rivera station. Four instruments continuously measured the chemistry and physical properties of airborne particles, allowing researchers to track rapid changes that can be missed by standard sampling methods, which collect particles over 24-hour periods every few days and analyze them weeks or months later.
The researchers also compared the Eaton Fire data with measurements from the Airport Fire, which burned 24,000 acres of vegetation in Riverside County in September 2024.
As the Eaton Fire moved from developed areas into the San Gabriel Mountains, its chemical signature shifted toward that of a more typical wildfire, the study found.
“Essentially, this comparison between the two fires indicates how different and chemically distinct an urban fire is,” Baliaka said.
Lead levels spiked across eastern Los Angeles and the San Gabriel Valley on Jan. 8 and 9, with the highest readings downwind of Altadena. The ratio of potassium to lead in the plume increased as the fire moved into the mountains, approaching wildfire-like levels by Jan. 11 and rising further the next day, according to the study.
Researchers said the health effects of short-term exposure to high concentrations of lead and other toxic chemicals remain unknown. The findings could help improve models used to predict where smoke and pollutants will travel during fires and guide emergency responses, according to Caltech.

sources.news_title: Smoke from LA fires exposed millions to high levels of toxic heavy metals
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES — At the height of the Los Angeles fires in 2025, millions of residents were exposed in a 24-hour period to toxic lead levels from smoke that were 80 times higher than the typical background level, according to a new study.
Researchers from the California Institute of Technology compared the chemical composition of smoke from the Eaton Fire with that of a wildfire and found that the urban plume had more lead, arsenic and halogens (which include chlorine and bromine) linked to burning vehicles, building materials and electronics.
“The main, key finding is really that wildfire smoke is very different fundamentally from the urban smoke,” said Nga Lee “Sally” Ng, an author of the study published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances. With the new technology they used to measure what was in the smoke, they were able to “actually see the very detailed component of these particles that we are breathing.”
Co-author Haroula Baliaka said understanding the different chemical compositions of smoke from an urban versus a wildland fire helps bridge a missing gap in research. Wildfires are growing larger, more intense, faster-moving and more frequent largely because of drier and warmer weather associated with human-caused climate change. As urban growth and climate change push more fires into cities, researchers said monitoring and emergency response will have to adapt.
Ed Avol, professor emeritus in the Keck School of Medicine at the University of Southern California who has researched the health effects of air pollution for decades, said significant exposure to heavy metals is consistent with what he'd expect, “but certainly surprising because we haven’t been able to document this sort of thing.”
“One of the real advantages of this study is that it had the opportunity to make measurements sort of hour-by-hour across the sampling network. And typically we make measurements of airborne particulates and so forth a couple of times a week, at best,” said Avol, who wasn’t involved in the study.
Thousands of structures burned, releasing toxic chemicals
The two wind-whipped infernos in Altadena and the Pacific Palisades that ignited on Jan. 7, 2025, killed at least 31 people and destroyed more than 16,000 structures, mostly homes, and everything in them — cars, paint, furniture, chemicals under sinks and more. Millions of people were exposed to smoke, which across the entire United States has been linked to tens of thousands of deaths annually. A recent study found that metal mixtures in the leftover smoke, ash and debris from the deadly 2023 Maui wildfires were harmful to the lung health of people living nearby long after the burning ended.
During the fires, researchers measured trace elements of fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, every hour reported by instruments in the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork ( ASCENT ), a relatively new network of air quality monitors across the U.S. that measures the size and chemical composition of these particulates in real time. Ng said ASCENT is the U.S.'s first measurement network able to measure the chemical composition of airborne particles in real time.
Researchers were able to see what chemicals were in the smoke, track how its composition changed over the fire's course, and distinguish emissions coming from burning structures. From there, they estimated how many people across Los Angeles were exposed to the heavy metals, particularly lead, during the fire's first days.
They compared the typical value of lead before the fires and the chemical makeup of smoke from a 2024 fire in Riverside County that burned mostly vegetation with data from the Eaton Fire plume. Contrasted with the wildfire smoke, the plume from the LA fire contained 50 times more lead, three times more arsenic, and seven times more halogens. At the peak of burning, about 7 million people were exposed for 24 hours to lead levels more than 80 times what's typical.
Lead is a neurotoxin that can stunt children’s development, lower IQ scores and increase blood pressure in adults. Scientists still don’t know how short-term, high exposure to lead impacts human health. Arsenic exposure is associated with various cancers.
Yaguang Wei, assistant professor in the department of environmental medicine at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai who researches the health impacts of air pollution, wildfire smoke and severe weather, said their findings reinforced some conclusions of a recent study he co-authored that found, in part, that PM2.5 from wildfire smoke was more toxic than particulates from other sources.
“I think their findings are not surprising,” said Wei, who was not involved in the study. When fires burn properties, they're also burning “a lot of lead on your wall paint and the plastics and electronics and those are very toxic” when they burn, he said.
Monitoring, policies and emergency response need to adapt, experts say
Wei said the study has “important policy implications.” He thinks governments should take stronger actions to protect public health during these fires by investing in more wildfire monitoring and public alerts, and having more prescribed fires.
For Avol, the study is a reminder of our “strange and increasingly dangerous new world” where urban and wildland intersect — and increasingly catch fire.
“It reminds us to be cautious and be concerned and, you know, think about what we can do to minimize this. We’re not going to stop using all these materials containing metals and halogens and so forth in our homes,” he said. “How do we protect people from being exposed to that?”

sources.news_title: L.A. fires exposed millions to lead levels way above normal, study says
Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
Eaton Wildfire Exposed Millions to a “Cocktail of Chemicals”
sources.text:
The January 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles killed 19 people, forced the evacuation of more than 100,000 others, and destroyed upward of 9,000 structures.
New research published today in Science Advances also shows that compared to the plume of smoke from a nonurban wildfire, its smoke—breathed in by millions in the area—had 50 times as much lead, 7 times the halogens, and 3 times as much arsenic.
Michael Kleeman, a civil and environmental engineer at the University of California, Davis, who was not involved in the research, said in an email to Eos these measurements represented, to his knowledge, the first real-time monitoring of toxicity levels in a large urban fire smoke plume.
“The real-time metals measurements showed without a doubt that the burning buildings and vehicles in these fires were generating toxic chemicals that have unique health risks,” he said. “The measurements described in this study brought into focus one of our next air quality challenges: how to handle risks from large urban fires that will become more common in a warming climate.”
The new research is based on data recorded by the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork (ASCENT), a network of 12 air quality monitors across the United States that provide continuous measurements of ambient levels of PM2.5, or particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers in diameter.
Traditionally, air quality is measured at specific points in time, such as on an hourly or daily basis, said Nga Lee “Sally” Ng, an aerosol scientist at California Institute of Technology (Caltech) and one of the paper’s authors. Though that might paint a broad picture of pollutant levels over a period, it doesn’t capture short-term temporal evolution or spikes that might occur during an event like a fire.
“You would not be able to detect that the lead or [other] toxins are at very high levels during specific times during the L.A. fires,” Ng explained. “ASCENT provides this real-time data to allow us to better understand the health impacts of short-term exposure to high levels of air pollutants.”
Divergent Chemistries
Previous research examined air quality following the fires, finding, for example, that one area downwind of the Eaton Fire saw lead levels up to 250 times higher than background levels during the fire.
The new paper contrasted what it called the “cocktail of chemicals” in the smoke not just with background levels, but with the levels found in a nonurban wildfire.
To make the comparison, researchers compared ASCENT data captured during the January 2025 Eaton Fire to that of a September 2024 fire in Riverside, Calif., that predominantly burned vegetation rather than urban area. The two wildfire plumes showed similar amounts of PM2.5, but their chemistries were vastly different. The Eaton Fire contained about 7 times as much chlorine and bromine, 4 times as much zinc, more than 3 times as much copper and arsenic, and, most remarkably, 50 times as much lead.
Inhaling bromine or chlorine can lead to coughing, dizziness, and even respiratory failure. Arsenic is a confirmed carcinogen. And according to the World Health Organization, no level of lead exposure is known to be harmless.
A New Database
The differences identified in the Eaton Fire’s plume chemistry come down to its fuel. First, there are the actual structures: houses with lead paint, wooden fences treated with preservatives containing arsenic, and plumbing pipes made of polyvinyl chloride (PVC). Then, there’s everything inside of those structures.
“Think of a typical household: the cleaning supplies under the sink, the plastic bins in the garage, the gas stove, the furniture, the car parked outside. Now multiply that by thousands of homes burning at once,” Haroula Baliaka, a Ph.D. student, first author of the study and an atmospheric scientist at Caltech, wrote in an email to Eos.
The paper’s publication is timely. Earlier this week, the team also published an ASCENT database that provides open access to all of the monitoring network’s data. The site offers two options to view: fully validated data from 2023 to 2024 and real-time air quality data.
“We are excited to share this data with the community and hope that this information can allow us to better understand the aerosol chemistry and physics as well as their impacts on climate and human health,” Ng said. “We also hope that, eventually this type of information can give us the knowledge to design future policies to better protect human health.”
—Emily Gardner (@emfurd.bsky.social), Deputy Editor

sources.news_title: LA wildfire smoke exposed 7 million to dangerous toxic metals
sources.text:
LA wildfire smoke exposed 7 million to dangerous toxic metals
A catastrophic 2025 Los Angeles firestorm exposed some 7 million people to high levels of airborne lead and other toxic metals released from burning homes and vehicles, according to a new study.
Scientists for the first time were able to quantify in real time the chemical composition of wildfire smoke thanks to a sensor network that went online months before the January 2025 Eaton conflagration that destroyed more than 9,400 buildings, killing 19 people.
As climate change triggers urban firestorms like the inferno in the LA suburb of Altadena, the paper published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances offers the first indication of how the incineration of homes, electronics, cars and infrastructure could affect even people who live far from the burn zone due to wind-blown toxic smoke.
The researchers determined that over a 24-hour period, smoke from the fire contained 80 times the concentration of lead normally found in the atmosphere. Lead is a neurotoxin linked to an array of health effects and is particularly harmful to children. Sensors also detected highly elevated levels of arsenic and other toxins. The smoke plume covered eastern LA and the San Gabriel Valley and affected about 70% of the county’s population.
Nga Lee (Sally) Ng, a co-author of the study and a professor of environmental science and engineering at the California Institute of Technology, said that while chronic exposure to metals like lead is well-studied, the health effects from short-term exposure to highly concentrated airborne toxins remains largely unknown.
“The hope is that with these real-time measurements, we can better understand and characterize the health impacts of these short-term exposures,” she said.
The data on Eaton was collected by a Los Angeles monitoring site that happened to be downwind of the fire. It’s part of the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry Measurement Network (ASCENT) that has established stations across the country. Ng, who is a principal investigator for the National Science Foundation-funded project, said the LA site wasn’t able to collect data on the Palisades fire, which ignited 34 miles away from the Eaton site hours earlier, due to the wind direction.
ASCENT also allowed the researchers to track how the toxic composition of the smoke plume changed over time as the fire burned, according to Haroula Baliaka, the study’s lead author who was a PhD candidate at Caltech at the time. That could help health researchers pinpoint health impacts from urban firestorms.
She said the study results should encourage policymakers to rethink strategies for evacuating residents from urban wildfires, given toxic smoke exposure can occur far from the burn zone. “I can envision that in the future we have these evacuation zones for smoke exposure as well,” said Baliaka. “Unfortunately, this is not a one-time event. It’s a new reality and we need to adapt to it and we need to do it sooner rather than later.”

sources.news_title: LA fire that devastated Altadena unleashed surge of toxic airborne metals
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES (CN) — The 2025 Eaton fire killed 19 people and destroyed more than 9,000 structures, including nearly all of the neighborhood of Altadena, California. It also, according to a new study, unleashed an “urban smoke plume,” exposing nearby residents to potentially harmfully high levels of airborne lead, arsenic and halogens.
“Millions of residents faced an acute toxic metal burden with unknown health consequences,” writes Caltech PhD student Haroula Baliaka and her colleagues. “Understanding and ultimately mitigating these health risks must become a priority as such [urban] events grow more frequent and severe.”
According to the paper, published Wednesday in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances, the Eaton fire contained a “cocktail of chemicals,” far more dangerous than recent wildfires in less urban areas.
“Compared to wildfire smoke, the urban plume was enriched more than 50-fold in lead, 7-fold in halogens, and 3-foldin arsenic, a toxic mixture linked to burning vehicles, electronics and building materials, a fundamentally different fuel from conventional wildland vegetation,” Baliaka and her colleagues write. “During peak structural burning, we estimate that approximately 7 million residents experienced 24-hour lead concentrations exceeding 50 nanograms per cubic meter, over 80 times background levels.”
The paper is an offshoot of Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork, or ASCENT, a network of 12 monitoring stations funded by the National Science Foundation. One of those monitoring stations is in Pico Rivera, an LA neighborhood about 18 miles south of the Eaton fire.
When Baliaka looked at the data from the monitoring station following the deadly blaze, what she saw surprised her. The chemicals from the smoke were completely different from a typical wildfire. There wasn’t nearly as much potassium; and there was far more lead.
“I was surprised by the magnitude and complexity, as far as chemicals were concerned,” Baliaka said in a recent phone interview. “In retrospect, it absolutely makes sense. When you think of everything you ave in your home — multiply that by thousands.”
Baliaka and her colleagues argue the Eaton fire represents a new kind of natural disaster that will only become more common, as urban sprawl and climate change cause more conflagrations with man-made sources of fuel. These fires will create a “chemically distinct class of air pollution” that our current air monitoring infrastructure is not set up to measure. Nor do researchers understand the impacts of short-term exposure to this kind of air pollution.
“While the toxicity of chronic exposure to individual elements is well established, far less is known about the consequences of these short-duration but high-intensity exposures, as well as the cumulative effects of simultaneous exposure to complex mixtures,” the authors of the paper write. “There is an urgent call for epidemiological studies to explore the health outcomes associated with these exposures, particularly in children and other vulnerable populations.”
“Our emergency responses should potentially change,” Baliaka said in the interview. “We don’t evacuate for smoke exposure, for example. We should just be having these conversations.”
The Eaton fire was caused by a decades-old idle power line, owned by Southern California Edison, that had been disconnected from the electrical grid for more than half a century. On Jan. 7, 2025, abnormally high gusts of winds pushed nearby live transmission lines to momentarily reactivate the so-called “zombie line,” temporarily electrifying it. Because the zombie line was surrounded by overgrown, dry vegetation, a fire erupted, with disastrous consequences.
More than 10,000 plaintiffs have sued Edison in an action that has been consolidated into one mass tort proceeding in downtown LA. The first bellwether trial is currently scheduled to begin in January 2027. The U.S. Justice Department has also sued Edison in federal court, while hundreds of plaintiffs have also sued State Farm, accusing it of underpaying claims.

Yaguang Wei, assistant professor in the department of environmental medicine at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai who researches the health impacts of air pollution, wildfire smoke and severe weather, said their findings reinforced some conclusions of a recent study he co-authored that found, in part, that PM2.5 from wildfire smoke was more toxic than particulates from other sources.
“I think their findings are not surprising,” said Wei, who was not involved in the study. When fires burn properties, they’re also burning “a lot of lead on your wall paint and the plastics and electronics and those are very toxic” when they burn, he said.
Monitoring, policies and emergency response need to adapt, experts say
Wei said the study has “important policy implications.” He thinks governments should take stronger actions to protect public health during these fires by investing in more wildfire monitoring and public alerts, and having more prescribed fires.
For Avol, the study is a reminder of our “strange and increasingly dangerous new world” where urban and wildland intersect — and increasingly catch fire.
“It reminds us to be cautious and be concerned and, you know, think about what we can do to minimize this. We’re not going to stop using all these materials containing metals and halogens and so forth in our homes,” he said. “How do we protect people from being exposed to that?”
